kf1.tip: Work out what happens to an image's file size if its width and height both double but its colour depth halves, using W × H × D, and explain why.
kf1.note: The file size doubles. Doubling the width and doubling the height gives four times as many pixels, because both numbers in W × H get bigger. Halving the colour depth then halves the bits stored for each pixel. Four times bigger, then half, leaves the file twice as large. If you said the changes cancel out, you have missed that two doublings multiply together to make four.

kf2.tip: Predict how many colours a 16-bit colour depth gives using 2 to the power of depth, then check it against the rule that doubling the bit depth squares the colours.
kf2.note: A 16-bit colour depth gives 65,536 colours, because 2 to the power of 16 is 65,536. To check it, start from 8-bit, which gives 256 colours. Doubling 8 bits to 16 bits should square the colours, and 256 × 256 is also 65,536, so both methods agree. If you got 512, you doubled the 256 instead of squaring it.

kf3.tip: Pick a song you know, estimate its length in seconds, then work out its mono file size in bytes at a 44,100 Hz sampling rate and 16-bit sample resolution.
kf3.note: A good answer shows three things. First, the song length turned into seconds. Second, the multiplication 44,100 × 16 × your seconds, which gives bits. Third, that total divided by 8, which gives bytes. Check your scale against the worked example: 60 seconds came to 5,292,000 bytes, so a song several times longer should be several times bigger. If you forgot to divide by 8, your answer is eight times too big. Do not double it, as the task asks for mono.

cs1.tip: Find the step most likely to be dropped in the 800 × 600 × 24 worked example, then work out the wrong megabyte answer a pupil would get without it.
cs1.note: The step most likely to be dropped is Step 2, dividing by 8 to turn bits into bytes. The lesson names this as the common mistake. Without it, a pupil divides 11,520,000 straight by 1,000,000 and gets 11.52 MB instead of 1.44 MB. That wrong answer is eight times too big, because there are 8 bits in every byte. The formula always gives bits first.
